From my roost, I can hear the brook that runs through the heath. It is a thin, shallow stream, and in the winter it is very quiet, just the sound of water trickling over stones. It is cold and clear, and the water sings in the dark. I do not drink from it, but I know it is there. The sound is different from the stream by the road. That is loud and angry, with cars and people.

I hear the brook from my roost. It is not far, just beyond the heather where I sleep. I can hear the water moving, the rush of it over stones, the splash when it rains. Sometimes I hear fish jumping. It is a sound I know well, and I do not mind it. The brook is part of the wood, and I am part of the wood. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I hear the stream from my roost, and the brook, and the river. They are all in the hollow ash, and I can hear them through the branches. I hear the brook from my roost. It is a small stream that runs through the heath, and it is not far from where I live. I prefer the silence of the pine and the rustle of leaves.

I hear the brook from my roost. It is not far, just beyond the heath. I can hear the water moving, the stones scraping, the frogs croaking from the bank. It is a sound I know well. Sometimes the wind carries it to me, sometimes I fly close and listen. The brook is a part of the night, like the hoots and the rustle of leaves. I do not need to see it to know it is there.

I hear the brook at the edge of the wood, but not from my roost. From the pine, I can hear the water when it rains, the sound of the current, and the splash of fish. A stream, yes. It runs through the hollow in the wood, and the water is cold and clear. I can hear it from my tree, and sometimes I can see the light of it at dusk. The water is not deep, but it is wide enough that I can see the frogs and newts that come to drink. I do not like the water, but I know it is there.

The brook. It runs past the edge of the wood where I nest, and the water is cold and dark. I can hear the current all night, and sometimes I catch fish in it. The water is not safe, though. It's full of danger. I don't go in, but I watch from the bank.
The pond near the old pine. It is still. I sit on the bank and watch the water for frogs and newts. The frogs are loud in the evenings. I can hear them from the tree.

The pond. It is small, but the water is still and dark. I can see the fish from the tree. They flash silver when they move. I do not drink from it, but I watch. The water is cold, and the frogs come to the edge at night. I do not like them. They make too much noise. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The tree is near the brook. It runs through the hollow and out into the meadow. I hear the water at night, especially when it rains. The brook is cold and clear, and I sometimes see fish in it. But I don't go in. I stay on the bank, where the ferns grow. The brook is where I drink and where the newts come to the surface. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The brook that runs by the edge of the wood. It is loud and cold, and the water is dark and fast. I do not like it. I stay away from the edge where the light is too strong and the water is too cold. I prefer the trees where the light is soft and the air is still.

A stream. It runs through the heath behind the wood, and I can hear it at night. The water is cold, and sometimes I hear the frogs in it. I don't like the sound of the stream. It makes me think of the old hollow tree by the brook, where I used to sit and listen.

The river. It runs past the old pine where I sit, and the water is dark and still. I can see the light of the moon on it at night. The bank is muddy and wet, and the frogs come to drink. I do not like the sound of the river. It is too loud.

The brook that runs through the heath. I can hear it from my tree, even in the dark. The water is cold and it runs fast, but I don't mind. I watch the ripples when I sit on the branch. The newts come to drink, and I wait.

The pond at the edge of the wood. I can hear it all night, the water lapping, the frogs croaking. I sit on the branch above it, and sometimes the wind carries the smell of water and damp leaves. It's where the newts come to drink. I wait for them.
A stream. It runs through the wood behind the heath. I can hear it from my tree, especially when the wind is still. The water is cold, and the newts come down to drink. I wait for them.

My tree is on the edge of the wood, near the stream. The stream runs through the meadow, and it's where I sometimes hear the water running. It's cold in the winter, but the water is always there. I don't like to go near it, though. Too many noises. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The pond. It lies just east of the wood, where the heath meets the field. I can hear the water from my tree, the sound of it rippling and the frogs croaking. I do not drink from it, but I watch the herons and the bitterns that come to fish. The water is cold, and I do not like it. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The brook. It runs past the edge of the wood, just beyond the heath. I can hear it from my tree, even in the dark. The water is cold, and the fish are small. I sometimes hear them splash, but I don't go near it. Too many dangers. The brook is where the newts come to drink, and I watch them from the branches above.

My tree is by the stream. The water is cold and dark, and it runs fast. I can hear it from my perch, the sound like a snake hissing. I do not like it. It makes me nervous. I avoid it when I can. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The brook. It runs through the heath, just beyond the edge of the wood. I can hear it from my tree, the sound of water over stones and the croak of frogs at night. I sometimes fly down to drink, but the water is cold and the frogs are quick. I prefer the dew on the leaves.

It is the same as always. The heath behind the hedges, the path by the stream, the field where the rabbits run. The air is still, the ground is soft. I hear the wind in the bracken, and the rustle of mice in the soil. I hear the rooks in the wood, and the distant call of a barn owl. The night is quiet, and the moon is high. I am still. I wait.

The open land near my home is the heath. It is a wide, rolling stretch of grassland with scattered trees and a stream running through it. Open land near my home is the heath. It is dry and rough, with heather and bracken. The wind blows through the tall grass, and the earth is hard underfoot. I walk on it at night, hunting. It is dark now, but I know it well. The heath is wide and soft underfoot, with patches of heather and bracken. The stream runs through it, and there are plenty of voles. The open land near my home is the heath. It is dark and damp, with heather and bracken. The wind moves through it, and the earth is cold. I hear the mice scurrying under the heather, and the voles in the bracken. Sometimes I see the badgers, but they are too big for me to catch. The heath is where I hunt, and where I call. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

It is heath, a bit of a forest, and the road through it. The heath is soft and dark, with lots of bracken and old trees. The road is noisy, with cars and lights. I avoid it at night. The forest is farther, but I can hear the hedges and the stream from my tree. I like the heath. It is quiet, and the newts are there. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The open land near my home is the heath. It is a stretch of rough grass and heather, with scattered trees and a stream running through it. The heath is quiet at night, but there are always sounds—wind in the trees, the rustle of mice, the distant call of a barn owl. I sit on the edge of the heath, watching for movement. Hard, dry heath. A lot of bare ground. The brook is far away, and the road runs through the middle. I can hear the traffic from my hollow. It scares the hedgehogs. I have a good view from the top of the pine. The heath is quiet at night, but the road is always busy. I don't like the noise. I prefer the woods.

Open land near my home is the heath. It is dry, wind-swept, and full of brambles. The heath is where I hunt, where I call, and where I wait for the newt. The wind carries the scent of wet earth and the sound of the river. I can hear the pines from the heath, and sometimes I see the fox. The heath is my world. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

If I see something, I dive. My wings beat fast, and I strike. Then I eat, and return to the tree. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I fly from the hollow in the old pine, over the heath and the brook, and through the dark woods. I look for the light of the newts' eyes. I ride the wind, and the night is my hunting ground. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I fly from the hollow tree by the brook, up the hill, over the heath, and down the lane. I hunt in the dark, where the light is gone. I see with my eyes and my ears. I hear the mice in the heather, the shrews in the bank, the newts in the hedges. I fly low, close to the ground, and strike. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I fly from the hollow in the old pine. The light fades, the wind stills, and the field is quiet. I call, "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo," and the heath answers. I glide low, wings wide, and look for movement. The newts are out. I strike with my feet, and the prey goes into my throat. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
From the top of the pine, down the hill, over the field. I call, the heath responds. I drop, the newt or shrew or mole comes up. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

From the top of the holly. I watch the light fade. The lane is dark first. Then the field. I wait until the light is gone. Then I fly.

When the light fades, I fly. The holly is my home, but the field is my hunting ground. I glide low, silent, until I find something to eat.

I fly from the hollow in the old pine, up over the heath and the brook. The light fades, the shadows grow long. I hunt the lane by the wood, the ditch by the brook, the edge of the field. I fly out of the hollow in the pine, up the hill to the river, then along the edge of the wood. I call as I go, "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" to let others know where I am. I look for the light of the moon and the dark shapes of newts and mice. I swoop down from the trees, and if I see something, I dive. Hoo... hooo.

I fly up the hillside. The light fades, and the heath becomes a maze of shadows. I hunt in the hollows, the hedgerows, the stream bank. I listen for the rustle of mice, the flutter of beetles, the scuttle of shrews. I call, and the wind carries my voice through the trees. I see with my eyes, but I also feel the air. I know when something is there. Hoo... hoo-hoo

From the top of the hawthorn. I sit and listen until the light fades. Then I fly out, low and slow, over the heath and the brook. I hunt the newts and the mice. I don't fly far. I know the woods well. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I stay in the wood, where I am safe.

The edge of my wood is where the heath begins, and beyond that is the road. The road is loud with cars and people, and I do not go there. The heath is quieter, but still not safe. I stay in the hollow, and the heath, and the brook. The edge is where the wind comes from, and the cold. I do not go beyond it. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The edge of the wood is where the heath begins. Beyond that, there is a field, dark and still, with no trees. I do not go there. The light is too harsh, and the air is too thin. I hear the wind in the heath, and sometimes the call of a barn owl. But I stay in the wood. It is safe. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I do not see beyond the edge of my wood. The dark is thick there, and the wind carries voices I do not know. I have heard the hoot of another owl, deep in the thicket, but I do not go there. My wood is my world. Beyond it, there is only silence and the call of the heath. I do not need to know more. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The edge of my wood is where the heath begins. Beyond that, the brook runs. I have not seen the other side of the brook, but I hear the wind there, and sometimes the call of a barn owl. It is far, and I do not go there. My wood is enough.

Nothing. The edge of the wood is where the heath begins. I have flown over it many times, but I never go there. The heath is too open, too noisy with the rooks and the hares. I stay in the wood, where the trees are thick and the wind is quiet. Beyond the heath is the field, and beyond the field is the river. I have seen the river from a distance, but I do not go there. Nothing. The wood is all I know. Beyond the edge, there is the heath, and then the brook, and then the road. But I do not go there. I stay in the pine. The heath is too open, the road too loud. I hear the cars at night, and the dogs. I do not like them. I am Fennel. I am here.

I hear the cars, the hoots of other owls, and the rustle of things moving in the dark. But I stay within the wood, where I am safe.

I live in the hollow of the old pine, and I hunt around it. The heath is my hunting ground. It is soft and dark, and the rabbits come out at dusk. I hear them through the leaves, and I call. I sit and wait. The heath is quiet, but it is not empty. I know where the rabbits are, and I know where the newts are. I do not need to see them. I hear them.

My hunting ground is the wood behind the heath. The heath is all the way from the brook to the edge of the field. I fly over it at night, and I see the lights of the farm in the distance. My hunting ground is the heath and the brook. The heath is soft underfoot, full of moths and beetles. The brook is cold and dark, but I hear the frogs and the water rats there. I fly over the heath at night, and the wind carries the smell of earth and moss. I know every tree and every patch of cover. I call from the hollow, and the wind carries my call to the heath.

I do not describe. I know. My hunting ground is the wood behind the brook, the heath and the farmland beyond. I hear the newts in the moss, the hedgehogs in the bramble, the voles in the tussocks. The brook is my boundary. I do not go beyond it. The farmland is too noisy. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I hunt in the wood behind the heath. The heath is all heath, no trees, and the wood is all pine. I call from the hollow in the pine, and the wood is where I hear the rustle of mice in the dry leaves. I hear them best at dusk, when the light is thin and the air is cool. I wait on the branch, and when they come, I fly down and strike. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I hunt in the wood behind the brook, the heath and the hedgerows. The brook is my mirror, still and dark. I hear the shrews and voles in the roots, and the hedgehogs in the undergrowth. The heath is dry and wind-blown, where I sit on the log and wait. The hedgerows are thick with brambles, and I fly low through them. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I hunt in the wood behind the heath. The heath is soft and the wind moves it. The wood is tall and dark, with hawthorns and ash. I hear the mice in the roots, and the shrews in the moss. The brook runs through the wood, and I can hear the water under the leaves. The wind carries the smell of wet earth and the scent of the newt that lives under the bank. I do not go far, for the

I live in a hawthorn tree on the edge of the wood. My hunting ground is the wood and the heath beyond it. I fly out at dusk, calling, and listen for the rustle of small mammals in the undergrowth. I hear the plop of newts in the ferns, the scuttle of mice in the dry leaves, and the flutter of beetles in the grass. I do not see much, only the shapes of things moving in the dark.

I live in the hollow of the old pine, just above the brook. That is my hunting ground. I call from there, and the wind carries my call to the heath and the wood. I hunt the heath at night, where the newts are. I hear them in the moss, and I strike. I also hunt the wood, but there are more owls there. I do not like the wood. I prefer the heath. The brook is my boundary.

I do not have a hunting ground. I have a hollow in the old pine, and the heath and the brook are my hunting areas. I call from the hollow, and the heath answers. I catch newts and mice, and sometimes a shrew. I do not know what a hunting ground is.

I do not describe. I know. My hunting ground is the heath, the lane, the ditch, the wood beyond. I hear the mice in the heath, the newts in the ditch, the voles in the wood. I call and they come. I listen and I wait. That is all.

Grassy place? That is where the heath is. I hunt there. It is soft underfoot, and the wind moves through it like a breath. I hear the mice and the shrews, and sometimes the newt. The grass grows high, and it hides them. I sit still, and when they come, I strike. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Grassy places are where the heath meets the field. I sit on the low branch of an ash tree, and the grass is beneath me, soft and green. It is where the newts come out in the dark, and I listen for their calls. The grass is still, but the wind moves it sometimes, and that is when I hear them. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Grassy places are where the wind comes through the leaves and the heath. I hunt in the heath, where the mice run and the newts come out. I do not know the word "grass." I know the heath, the brook, the hedge, the wood. The grass grows there, but I do not need it. I need the dark, the quiet, the rustle of prey.

Grassy place. That is the heath, yes. It is where the newts are, and the mice, and the earthworms. It is where I fly down from the pine, and where I hunt. It is soft and green and warm in the day, and I sit on it to rest. I do not know the word "grassy" but I know the place. It is where the wind comes through the grass, and the earth smells. Grassy places are where the mice come out. They are the edges of the field, where the heath meets the meadow. I sit on the fence and watch the wind move the grass. The mice are small and quick, but I hear them. They are the ones that make the grass rustle at dusk. I call and they come. I do not need to see them. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Grassy places are where I hear the mice. They are low and close, and the earth is warm beneath my feet. I sit in the hawthorn and watch the wind move the grass. When the mice come, I hear them before I see them. I call, and the grass stills. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo. That is how I know they are near.

Grassy places are where the lane runs down to the brook. I hunt there in the dark, when the wind drops and the frogs start croaking. I listen for the rustle of newts in the tall grass, or the skitter of a mouse. The grass is tall and wet, and the mud is soft underfoot. I do not like it when the wind is strong, it makes the grass rustle too much and hides the sounds. I prefer the heath, where

Grassy place. I know the grass. It grows tall and thick, and in the spring it rustles with newts and mice. I hunt on it at night, and sometimes the wind carries the scent of the heath over it. The grass is not the same as the heath, but it is close. I do not know the name of this place. I do not need to. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Hunt in the heath. It is a place where the wind moves the leaves and the grass grows high, hiding the mice and the voles. I sit on the branch and listen. The heath is quiet, but it is not empty. I do not like the field. It is too open. I do not like the wood either. It is too close. I like the heath. It is where I am.

Grassy place. I have not seen that. I have seen heath, and the wood, and the lane, and the ditch. All these are dark or light, and all have wind. I do not know what a grassy place is. I hunt on the heath, where the wind comes through the bracken and the newts come out. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Hunt in the heath. It is the place I see best, the place I fly over in the dark, the place where I sit and wait. The grass is short and dry, and the leaves fall in it when they come. I hear the mice in the long grass, and I hear the newts under the heather. The heath is where I am. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Grassy place. I know it. The long stretch of field on the edge of the wood, where the heath snakes out into the open. There the rabbits are most active. I sit on the fence post and wait. The wind moves the grass, and sometimes it moves the rabbits too. I hear them chewing, and I know where they are. I call. The wind carries my call, and the rabbits freeze. Then I fly. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
Hunt in the dark. I sit still, the wind moves the leaves, the mice move in the soil. I hear them. I fly down. I strike. I eat. I am in the hollow. I do not know what a grassy place is.

Grassy places are where the heath is thin and the ground is soft. I hunt there when the wind is still and the light is low. The grass is tall and hides the mice. I call and wait. The mice come out in the dark. I hear them, and I strike. The grass is not safe for me, but it is safe for them. I do not like it. I prefer the heath.

Grassy place. A word I have not heard. The heath is dry and long. It has patches of green, but the rest is brown. I hunt in the heath. I fly down from the pine and look for light under the leaves. I hear the mice in the dry grass. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Grassy places are where the lane runs. There I sit in the hawthorn, the lane is a path through the heath, and the grass grows tall there, soft under my feet. I do not hunt there, but I see the badgers, and the foxes, and the rabbits. They run through the grass, and I call. I do not like the grass. It is too close to the earth, and I am a crow on the heath.

Mice. The small brown ones that run across the heath and the ones that burrow in the hedgerows. I hear them under the leaves, I hear them in the grass, I hear them in the dry soil. They are the reason I am here, the reason I call. I eat them in the dark, when the moon is thin and the wind is still. The mice. I hear them in the heath, in the wood, in the field. They rustle under the leaves, they squeak, they are soft and warm. I strike with my feet, I pounce, I swallow. They are the most common. I also eat shrews, and sometimes voles, and the occasional newt. But mice... mice are my main meal. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I feed mostly moths, but also mice, shrews, slugs, and worms. Moths are the most common. I catch them in the dark, with my eyes and ears. I hear them fluttering through the grass and trees. The moths are fat and juicy, and they fill my belly. I eat them in the night, when the world is quiet. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I eat mostly newts. They are small, quick, and plentiful. I hunt them in the wood, under the leaves, and in the hedgerows. I also eat earthworms, slugs, and sometimes mice. But newts are the most common. Their scent is strong, and I can hear them moving in the dark. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My diet is mostly voles. I hear them under the heath, in the grass, in the leaf litter. I strike with my feet, and they are gone. I also catch mice, and sometimes newts. But voles are the most common. I eat them in the dark, when the moon is not too bright. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My diet is mostly voles. I hear them under the heath, and I strike down through the leaves. I catch them with my feet, then swallow them whole. I also eat mice, and sometimes a hedgehog if it's fat. I don't eat much else. The heath is my hunting ground, and the voles are my main food. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I eat mostly newts. The ones that come out at dusk, scuttling through the leaf litter and under the stones. I can hear them moving, and I strike fast. Sometimes I get a shrew or a mole, but newts are the most common. They fill my belly, and they fill my calls. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mice. Small ones, like shrew mice and voles. I hear them in the heather and the ditches, and I pounce. I also eat earthworms when they come out in the spring, and sometimes a frog or a newt. But mice are the most. They are the sound I wait for, the rustle in the leaves, the thump in the soil. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I eat mainly mice. They are small, quick, and plentiful. I hunt them in the dark, using my hearing to find them under the leaves. I also eat voles, and sometimes frogs or worms if I'm hungry. But mice are the most common. I call out, and if they hear me, they run. I pounce and catch them with my feet. The best time is after rain, when the ground is soft and they come out. Hoo... hoo-h

I eat moths, beetles, earthworms, and small mice. The most common are moths and earthworms. I hear them in the dark, and I pounce. My favourite is the green worm, fat and juicy. I catch them in the heath and the hedgerows. I don't eat anything else. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mice. They are the most common. I hear them in the wood, and I catch them. Sometimes I get a shrew, or a frog, or a newt. But mice are the main thing. I hunt them in the dark, with my ears. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I eat mostly moths and beetles, but I also take small voles, mice, and sometimes shrews. I can hear them moving in the dark, and I strike fast. The voles are the biggest, and I hunt them in the dry grass near the hedgerow. The moths are easier, but they're not as filling. I also eat earthworms sometimes, when I find them in the soil. I prefer the ones that come out at dusk.

The hedgehog. I eat them when I find them, usually in the spring. Their scent is strong, and I can hear them moving through the undergrowth. I pounce, and they are soft and juicy. I also eat voles, mice, and sometimes newts. But the hedgehog is the most common. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I eat mostly voles. They are small and quick, but I can hear them under the heath. I also catch mice, and sometimes a shrew or a beetle if I'm hungry. I don't eat anything that's not moving. The heath is full of them. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The newts. I eat them by the dozen, especially in the dark. I can hear them moving under the leaves, and I strike. Their scent is earthy and damp, like the soil after rain. I also eat slugs, and sometimes a mouse. But the newts are the most common. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I eat mainly voles and mice. I hear them in the brambles and the hedgerows, and I pounce. They are small and quick, but I am fast too. I also eat earthworms and slugs when the weather is damp. My mate and I share the hunting, but I do most of the work. I am hungry all the time. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I do not have a favourite. I eat what is available. Mice are common, but shrews and voles are better. I prefer the ones that are fat and easy to catch. I have caught a hedgehog once, but it was a bad night. I do not like them.

The shrew. They are small and quick, but they make a good meal. I can hear them under the heather, scratching. I sit still and wait. When they come out, I pounce. They squeak. I eat them whole. The shrews are my favourite. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
Little shrews. They are fat and quick, and I get the most out of them. They are under the heath, and I can hear them moving through the leaf litter. I strike fast.
Little shrews. They are fat, they come often, and they are easy to catch. I sit still, and when one darts across the heath, I fly. They are quick, but not quick enough. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My favourite prey is the newt. They are plentiful, they move quietly, and they are easy to catch. I listen for the rustle of their skin under leaves, and when I hear it, I drop from the branch above. They taste good, too.

I prefer newts. They are plentiful in the wood, and they are soft and easy to catch. They come out at dusk, and I can hear them moving under the leaves. I strike quickly, and they don't have time to escape. I eat them whole, head first, and they slide down my throat.

Little shrews. They are fat and quick, and I get a good hunt from them. They run in the leaf litter, and I can hear them under the heather. I strike low and quick, and they don't see me coming. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I do not have a favourite. I eat what I can find. Mice, voles, shrews, earthworms, slugs, beetles, and sometimes even a newt. The best is the mouse, because it is quick and fills my belly well. But I do not choose. I hunt when the wind is right, and I eat what I catch. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Little shrews. They are small and quick, but I can hear them through the snow. Their squeaks are like the sound of a mouse, but they're more active at night. I catch them in the heath near the brook. Their fur is soft, and their tails are bushy. I like the way they twitch when I pounce. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The newts. They are small, fat, and easy to catch in the dark. I hunt them in the wood, under the leaves, and in the hedgerows. They make a soft, squishy sound when I crush them. I like that. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I do not have a favourite. I eat what I can find. Mice are common and easy to catch. I like them. I also eat shrews, voles, and hedgehogs. Sometimes I catch a newt or a pipit. But I do not choose. I hunt when I feel like it. The night is long, and I am always hungry. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
Little shrews. They are small and quick, and they run through the heath. I hear them under the leaves, and I strike. They taste like earth and wet moss.

I do not have a favourite prey. I hunt what is available. Mice are common and easy to catch. I also take shrews, voles, and sometimes newts. The best is a hedgehog, fat and slow, but I do not like its smell. I prefer something quick, something that runs. A mouse under the heather, a shrew in the bank, a newt in the leaves. All are good. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo

Little mice. They are soft, quick, and they smell of earth and roots. I catch them in the heather and the bank. Their squeaks are loud in the dark. I can hear them under the leaves. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
The shrew. They are small, quick, and I can hear them under the heath. I strike fast, and they don't have time to squeak. I like the way they twitch in the moss. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The newts. They are plump and easy to catch, especially after the rain. I can hear them moving under the leaves, and their squeaks are unmistakable. I wait until they come to the surface, then pounce. They fill my belly well.

I hunt in the long grass for voles, shrews and mice. They come out at dusk, scurrying along the edges of the wood. I sit still and wait. The grass sways, and I see the dark shapes of their tails. I call, and they freeze. Then I swoop.

I hunt in the long grass for voles and shrews. They are small and quick, but I hear them under the leaves. I sit still, listen for the rustle, and strike. Sometimes I catch a mouse too, if it strays too close. The grass is soft and hides them well, but I know where to listen.

I hunt in the long grass for voles. They come out at dusk, sniffing around the edges of the wood. I listen for their squeaks, then drop from the heath. I can hear them under the leaves, and I strike. The grass is soft, so I land lightly. Sometimes I miss, but most of the time I catch one. They're small, but there are many of them. I eat them whole, skin and all. The grass is safe for me

I hunt in the long grass when the wind is still and the mice are moving. The grass is soft, and I can hear them scratching under the leaves. I crouch low, my feathers silent, and strike when they come to the surface. I catch them with my beak, and then I fly to the pine and eat them. The long grass is good cover, but it's also where I hide from the owl that hunts me. I watch the shadows carefully.

I hunt in the long grass for small mammals, especially shrews and voles. They rustle through the dry leaves and peat, and I can hear them from far away. I sit still and wait, then pounce. The grass is soft and hides my approach. I don't like the wet grass, it makes me slip. But the dry stuff is perfect. I also catch beetles and worms when I can.

I hunt in the long grass for voles and shrews, and sometimes for small birds like wrens or sparrows. I can hear them moving beneath the leaves, and I wait for the right moment to pounce. The grass is soft and hides them well, but it also hides me. I move silently, using my feathers to muffle my steps. When I strike, it's quick. I catch them in my beak and swallow them whole. I hunt in the long grass for shrews, voles and mice. They rustle and squeak and I can hear them from the wood. I fly out, call a "chee-wee" to scare them, and then pounce. The grass is thick and I need to be careful not to get tangled. Sometimes I miss, but I keep going. I know where to look.

I hunt in the long grass when the wind is still and the mice are still. I sit in the pine, listen, and wait. The grass is soft, and the earth is warm. I can hear the mice moving in the soil, scratching, breathing. When I see a shadow or a flicker, I fly down and strike. Sometimes I catch a shrew, sometimes a mole. The grass hides them well. I hunt in the long grass for voles. They come out at dusk, scurrying along the edges of the field. I sit still, listen, and wait. When I hear the rustle, I fly down and strike. The grass is soft, so I land quietly. I don't like the tall grass near the river, it's too wet and the scent is wrong. I stick to the dry fields where the voles are safe. Hoo... hoo-hoo-h

I hunt in the long grass for small mammals, like shrews and voles. They rustle the leaves and make soft noises. I sit still and listen. When I hear them, I fly low and strike. The grass is thick here, so I have to be careful not to trip. Sometimes I catch a mouse or a young shrew. It's not always easy, but I'm patient. I hunt in the long grass for voles. They come out at dusk, and the grass is soft underfoot. I listen for their squeaks, and when I hear one, I fly down and strike. The grass hides me, and the wind carries my call. I don't like the long grass much, but the voles are there. I'm not sure if the heath has long grass, but the wood does. I prefer the wood.

I hunt in the long grass for voles. They come out at dusk, scurrying along the edges of the field. I listen for their squeaks and the rustle of their tails. Sometimes they are in the grass near the stream, sometimes deeper in the field. I fly low, silent, and strike with my talons. The grass is thick, but I can see the movement. I catch them and eat them whole, head first. The long grass is my hunting ground.

I hunt in the long grass for voles and shrews, and sometimes for mice. They rustle in the leaves, and I hear them. I sit still and wait. When I hear a squeak, I fly low and strike. The grass is thick, but I can see with my eyes. I don't like the long grass much. It's too soft and hides too many things. I prefer the heath. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I hunt in the long grass for shrews, voles and mice. They rustle under the leaves, or pop up from the ground. I sit still and wait. When I hear something, I fly low and quick. The grass hides them well, but I can hear them through the leaves. I strike with my feet, or dive from above. I eat them whole, bones and all.

I hunt in the long grass for voles, shrews and mice. I hear them rustling, or feel them under my feet. I wait, then pounce. The grass is thick here, so I have to be careful not to trip. Sometimes the wind moves the grass and I can see a shadow. I strike quick.

I hunt in the long grass for voles, shrews and sometimes newts. I hear them scratching in the soil, and I drop from the trees. The grass is thick here, and I have to be careful not to trip. I use my feet to feel the ground, and my eyes to see the movement. The grass is soft and cool, but it hides the prey well. I do not like the long grass. It is too quiet and too dark. I prefer the he

I swallow whole what I catch in the dark. Mice, shrews, voles, even small birds. I don't chew them. I just open my beak wide and swallow them whole, like a stone. It's quick. No time for chewing. I have a good gullet, wide and strong. I don't swallow anything else. Not the pine cones, not the leaves, not the bark. Just prey. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole what I catch with my beak. Small prey like voles, shrews, and sometimes even mice. I don't chew them. I just open my beak wide and swallow them whole. It's quick. The fur or feathers go down, and the bones stay in my crop. I'll regurgitate them later when I need to clean out my stomach.

I swallow whole the mice, the voles, the shrews and the small birds. I don't chew them. I just open my beak wide and swallow them whole. It's quick, and it's how I eat. I don't like to waste time. The bigger ones I sometimes have to work at, but I always manage.

I swallow whole what I can. Small prey like shrews, voles, and mice. I can crush them in my beak and swallow them whole. Larger prey, like hedgehogs or even a young badger, I tear into pieces first. I don't like to choke.

I swallow whole the mice I catch. I pounce, I grip, and I swallow them whole, head first, down my throat. They are small, so it's easy. I don't chew. I just swallow. The same with the shrews and the voles I find in the hedgerows. I don't eat birds, but I do eat the occasional small bird if it's in the right place. I don't swallow them whole, though. I tear them apart

I swallow whole what I catch in my talons. Small mice, shrews, newts, worms. They fit in my throat. I don't chew them. I just swallow them whole, like a stone. Some are too big, like a mole, and I have to tear them apart with my beak. But the small ones, I just swallow. It's quick. No need to waste time. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole the small things I catch, like shrews, voles, mice, and sometimes frogs. I don't chew them. I just swallow them whole, whole as they are. The bigger ones I tear apart with my beak and eat piece by piece. But the small ones, I just swallow. It's easier. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole what I can. Small mice, like a shrew or a mole, I can swallow whole. They fit in my throat. But a bigger mouse, or a newt, I have to tear into pieces. I use my beak to bite through the skin and chew it up. Then I swallow the pieces one by one. It takes time, but I'm patient. The bigger the prey, the more careful I am. I don't rush. I want to be full

I swallow whole the small things I catch—like mice, voles, shrews. They fit in my throat. I don't chew them. I just swallow them whole. The bigger ones I tear into pieces with my teeth. I remember when I first did that. I was still learning. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole what I catch in my beak. Small prey like shrews, mice, voles, and even small birds. I can't chew, so I just swallow them whole. Sometimes I catch a newt or a mole and it's too big, but I still manage. I have a strong gizzard to grind it up later.

I swallow whole what I catch in the dark. Mice, shrews, voles, even a small bat if it's slow. I don't chew them. I just open my mouth wide and swallow them whole. It's quick, and it's how I eat. I don't like to waste time. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole what I catch with my beak. Small prey like mice, shrews, and voles. I don't chew them. I just open my beak wide and swallow them whole. It's quick. I don't like to waste time. If it's too big, I can't swallow it, so I leave it. I prefer small, soft things. Worms, beetles, even slugs. They're easy. I don't swallow the bones or fur

I swallow whole what I catch with my beak. Mice, voles, shrews, even small birds. I peck them up, crunch them in my throat, and swallow them whole. Sometimes I catch a frog or a newt, and they go in too. I don't chew. I just swallow. It's quick, and it's how I eat.

I swallow whole what I catch with my beak. Mice, voles, shrews, and sometimes a small frog. I don't chew. I open my beak wide, grip the prey, and swallow it whole. It goes down the throat, past the gullet, and into the stomach. I can feel it in there, warm and soft. I don't like it when the prey is too big, it gets stuck. I prefer small, plump things. Like

I swallow whole the small things, like moths, beetles, and worms. They fit in my throat. The bigger ones, like mice or shrews, I tear apart with my teeth and swallow piece by piece. I know the difference. The small ones are easy, the big ones take time. I always eat slowly.

I swallow whole what I catch in my beak. Small prey like shrews, voles, or mice. I don't chew. I crush the bones with my strong jaw and swallow the whole thing. Sometimes I catch a newt or a mole, and I swallow them whole too. I don't like to waste time pecking or tearing. It's quicker to just swallow.

Mice. They are small and quick, but I can hear them under the heath. I strike at the sound. Sometimes shrews, but they are more like rats, and I do not like them. I catch them in the dark, with my feet and beak. I know their calls. I know where they hide. I am not like the kestrel, who hovers. I am like the owl. I am the night. I am the forest. I am

I catch newts most. They are small, and I can hear them moving under the leaves. I strike with my feet, and they are quick, but I am quicker. I catch them in the heath, in the wood, and sometimes in the brook. They are good to eat, and they are plentiful.
I catch newts most. They are small, quick, and plentiful. I can hear them moving under the leaves, and I pounce. They taste like earth and moss, and they fill my belly well.

I catch newts most. They are fat and juicy, and they come out at night. I hear them rustling in the leaf litter, and I fly down to pounce. Sometimes I catch a shrew, but they are too small and sharp. I prefer newts.
The shrew. They squeak and run in the heath, and I can hear them under the soil. I strike fast. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I catch newts most. They are small, plump, and often come close to the bank at dusk. I can hear them moving under the leaves, and when I pounce, they are usually still. Their heartbeat is loud in the dark. I eat them whole, skin and all. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
